Its maximal cliques are tinted regions, A, B, C in the accent color, B, C, D in teal and D, E in violet, overlapping where they share nodes. The card lists them in the same colors: [A, B, C], [B, C, D], [D, E]." width="100%"} On a chordal graph (see `is_chordal()`) the maximal cliques can be found in linear time, and there are at most as many of them as nodes, whereas general graphs can have exponentially many. The cliques of a chordal graph are the bags of its clique tree (the junction tree used for exact inference in graphical models), and the largest one gives its treewidth plus one. Isolated nodes are cliques of size one. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The maximal cliques as sorted lists of node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed or not chordal. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A single maximum cardinality search per component: each newly numbered node with its numbered neighbors is a clique, and a clique is reported when the next one stops containing it. $O(V + E)$ besides the set operations. Matches NetworkX's `chordal_graph_cliques`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two triangles sharing an edge (a "diamond") plus a pendant node: ::: {#64fb356e .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) g.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E")]) [[g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in c] for c in g.chordal_graph_cliques()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['A', 'B', 'C'], ['B', 'C', 'D'], ['D', 'E']] ``` ::: :::
